# IEnumerable

`IEnumerable` (and its generic version `IEnumerable<T>`) is the **base interface** for all collections that can be iterated over in C#.


## What is IEnumerable?


Think of `IEnumerable<T>` as similar to:
- **Dart's `Iterable<T>`** - almost identical concept!
- **Python's iterable protocol** - anything you can loop over with `for...in`

It represents a **forward-only sequence** of elements that you can iterate through one at a time.


## The Collection Hierarchy


Here's how C# collections relate to each other:

```
IEnumerable<T>              ← Base interface (can iterate)
    ↓
ICollection<T>              ← Adds Count, Add, Remove, Contains
    ↓
    ├─→ IList<T>            ← Adds indexing [i], Insert
    │       ↓
    │       └─→ List<T>     ← Concrete dynamic array
    │
    ├─→ ISet<T>             ← Unique elements
    │       ↓
    │       └─→ HashSet<T>  ← Concrete hash set
    │
    └─→ IReadOnlyCollection<T>

IDictionary<K,V>            ← Key-value pairs
    ↓
    └─→ Dictionary<K,V>     ← Concrete hash map
```


## Core Interface: `IEnumerable<T>`


The interface only has **one method**:

```csharp
public interface IEnumerable<T>
{
    IEnumerator<T> GetEnumerator();
}
```

This is what enables the `foreach` loop:

```csharp
IEnumerable<int> numbers = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 };

foreach (int num in numbers)  // ← IEnumerable enables this
{
    Console.WriteLine(num);
}
```


## Comparing to Dart


Since you know Dart, here's a direct comparison:

```dart
// Dart
Iterable<int> numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
for (var num in numbers) {
  print(num);
}
```

```csharp
// C# - Almost identical!
IEnumerable<int> numbers = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 };
foreach (var num in numbers) 
{
    Console.WriteLine(num);
}
```


## Why Use IEnumerable?


**1. Flexibility** - Accept any collection type:

```csharp
// This method works with List, Array, HashSet, etc.
void PrintItems(IEnumerable<string> items)
{
    foreach (var item in items)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(item);
    }
}

// All of these work:
PrintItems(new List<string> { "A", "B" });
PrintItems(new string[] { "X", "Y" });
PrintItems(new HashSet<string> { "M", "N" });
```

**2. LINQ Support** - All LINQ methods work on `IEnumerable<T>`:

```csharp
IEnumerable<int> numbers = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 };

var evenNumbers = numbers.Where(n => n % 2 == 0);  // Like Dart's .where()
var doubled = numbers.Select(n => n * 2);          // Like Dart's .map()
```


## Key Characteristics


**Lazy Evaluation** - Similar to Dart's `Iterable`:

```csharp
IEnumerable<int> numbers = GetNumbers(); // Not executed yet
var filtered = numbers.Where(n => n > 10); // Still not executed!
var result = filtered.ToList(); // ← NOW it executes
```

**Forward-Only** - Can only iterate once in a streaming fashion:

```csharp
IEnumerable<int> numbers = ReadFromFile(); // Imagine this streams data

foreach (var num in numbers) { } // First iteration - OK
foreach (var num in numbers) { } // Second iteration - might fail or restart
```


## When You See IEnumerable in Code


```csharp
// Return type - means "I return a sequence"
public IEnumerable<User> GetActiveUsers()
{
    return users.Where(u => u.IsActive);
}

// Parameter type - means "I accept any collection"
public void ProcessItems(IEnumerable<Item> items)
{
    // Process items...
}
```


## Quick Practice


Try this on your Mac:

```csharp
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;

var fruits = new List<string> { "apple", "banana", "cherry", "date" };

// IEnumerable from LINQ query
IEnumerable<string> longFruits = fruits.Where(f => f.Length > 5);

foreach (var fruit in longFruits)
{
    Console.WriteLine(fruit);
}
```
